card.summary: H.R. 633, known as the TAKE IT DOWN Act, prohibits the nonconsensual online publication of intimate visual depictions of individuals, covering both authentic images and computer-generated digital forgeries. It requires covered online platforms to establish formal notice-and-removal processes and to remove reported content within 48 hours. Violators face criminal penalties, including fines and imprisonment, alongside mandatory restitution and forfeiture, while platforms that comply in good faith are protected from liability.

selection.reason: Impact scored and summarised by Gemini.

summary: The TAKE IT DOWN Act makes it a federal crime to publish or threaten to publish nonconsensual intimate visual depictions, including both authentic photos/videos and computer-generated digital forgeries (deepfakes) of adults and minors. It also requires public internet platforms that host user-generated content to create a clear process for individuals to request the removal of such images and to take them down within 48 hours of receiving a valid request.

affected_groups.effect: Gain legal tools to request prompt removal of these images from internet platforms within 48 hours and see offenders face criminal penalties.
affected_groups.group: Adults and minors whose intimate images or digital forgeries are published without consent

affected_groups.effect: Must create notice and takedown mechanisms, provide clear instructions for users, and remove flagged intimate depictions within 48 hours or face enforcement by the Federal Trade Commission.
affected_groups.group: Internet platforms and online services that host user-generated content

affected_groups.effect: Subject to criminal prosecution, fines, imprisonment up to 3 years depending on the offense, mandatory restitution, and property forfeiture.
affected_groups.group: Individuals who publish or threaten to publish nonconsensual intimate images or deepfakes

key_provisions: Prohibits the intentional online publication of nonconsensual intimate visual depictions of adults where the publisher intended to cause harm or caused psychological, financial, or reputational harm, and where the subject had a reasonable expectation of privacy.
Prohibits the online publication of intimate visual depictions of minors with the intent to abuse, humiliate, harass, degrade, or sexually gratify anyone.
Applies the same prohibitions and criminal penalties to computer-generated digital forgeries (deepfakes) that mimic authentic intimate images.
Prohibits intentional threats to publish intimate visual depictions or digital forgeries for the purpose of intimidation, coercion, extortion, or creating mental distress.

Mandates that individuals convicted under these provisions face criminal penalties (prison time, fines, or both), mandatory forfeiture of property used or gained in the offense, and mandatory restitution.

Requires covered platforms (websites, apps, or services primarily providing a forum for user-generated content) to establish a clear notice and takedown process for nonconsensual intimate images within one year of enactment.
Requires covered platforms to remove reported nonconsensual intimate visual depictions and make reasonable efforts to remove known identical copies within 48 hours of receiving a valid request.
missing_information: Specific dollar amounts for fines under Title 18, which are referenced generically in the text.
summary_detail.plain_summary: The TAKE IT DOWN Act makes it a federal crime to publish or threaten to publish nonconsensual intimate visual depictions, including both authentic photos/videos and computer-generated digital forgeries (deepfakes) of adults and minors. It also requires public internet platforms that host user-generated content to create a clear process for individuals to request the removal of such images and to take them down within 48 hours of receiving a valid request.
summary_detail.significance: This legislation establishes federal criminal penalties for sharing nonconsensual intimate images and artificial intelligence-generated deepfakes, while imposing strict 48-hour removal timelines on interactive internet platforms under Federal Trade Commission enforcement.
